More important, however, is not simply the assessment that underlying inflation has “reached 2%,” but how the BoJ distinguishes between reaching 2% and becoming firmly stabilized at around 2%. A judgment that underlying inflation has currently reached around 2% is not necessarily equivalent to a judgment that it will remain around that level going forward and that achievement of the price stability target has become sufficiently certain. records.text: on would mark a shift from recent ECB speak and likely be taken dovishly. In terms of hawkish risks to the front end, any messaging that downplays the impact of tighter financial conditions and instead stresses upside inflation risks, perhaps noting that energy prices are now well into the adverse scenario, would likely be taken hawkishly. Relatedly, the ECB could emphasise the separation between the policy rate and its other instruments, noting that it has dedicated tools to deal with fragmentation, implying that recent stress in EGB markets need not constrain further rate hikes. Finally, any indication that there was a strong debate around hiking already at this meeting, with at least some members favouring a move, would be seen as hawkish, as well. Would a QT pause/halt be a solution? To deal with potential broadening stress and/or fragmentation in EGB markets, the ECB has three potential options: (1) leaning more dovish on its policy rate communication; (2) an end or pause to QT in some shape or form; and (3) activation of the TPI/OMT . The significant negative correlation implies that occupation-level employment declines by an incremental 4% for each 1pp incremental increase in the overall unemployment rate. The right chart shows that occupation-level separation rates increase and that occupation-level job hiring rates decline when the labor market is weaker. These patterns can help explain why the labor market impacts have been smaller than feared so far: Given that the overall economy and labor market have remained resilient in 2026, companies may have had less incentive to focus on aggressively cutting labor costs. And under our baseline forecasts for near potential growth next year, our estimates suggest that AI labor disruption will likely only gradually increase rather than delivering an abrupt labor market shock. From a communication perspective, we expect the ECB to deliver a relatively balanced message, with plenty of 'on the one hand' and 'on the other hand' . On the one hand, it will need to acknowledge the further rise in energy prices, which has brought the outlook closer to the adverse scenario. On the other, given the recent rhetoric around tighter financial conditions, and the ongoing stress in EGBs, it will likely argue that these provide at least some offset. Which of the two forces receives greater emphasis will likely dictate whether the meeting is construed as hawkish or dovish. Naturally, where market pricing settles after Friday’s October flash PMIs will matter. Ahead of that refunding, term premium had risen sharply, the 2s30s curve had steepened and markets provided stronger evidence that investors were demanding additional compensation to absorb duration. FX: The major risks around the midterms – a downward correction in AI sentiment and a worsening fiscal position – would both put downward pressure on the USD, in our view. Should markets reassess the outlook of the AI buildout, we think it would be USD negative, despite the USD typically outperforming in periods of risk-off. This is for two reasons. For one, foreign investors have become large buyers of US equities in recent years, implying scope for active selling if US equities were to underperform. Second, foreign investors have also been more active in their FX hedging of US equities. As we think US stock–FX correlations would rise in an AI-related drawdown, foreign investors would likely increase their hedging of USD exposure. Given the US’s large need for foreign funding, a US- centric ‘fiscal-risk shock’ would be another headwind, suggesting risks to the USD are asymmetrically skewed lower into year end.

That said, there are two major risks to sentiment around the AI trade associated with the midterm elections. The first relates to the Democrats taking the House: Democratic control means there could be more investigations and subpoenas of AI companies and their CEOs, continuing to fuel public opposition to the AI buildout in an environment where the issue is increasingly bipartisan. The second, and more significant, would occur if there is a Democratic sweep, as we think this would likely increase market pricing of a unified Democratic government after the 2028 presidential election. Associated with this, the markets would also be likely to price in higher risks of anti-AI regulation from 2028 onward, which we think could adversely impact current valuations. records.text: M Idea 8 Another important issue in assessing the rationale for shorter intervals between rate hikes is how Governor Ueda reinforces the BoJ's assessment that current financial conditions remain accommodative. Recent data, including the Tankan, do not appear to indicate that the rate hikes implemented thus far have had a clear tightening effect on corporate financing conditions or corporate behavior. However, this line of argument is relatively backward-looking. If the BoJ intends to shorten the intervals between future rate hikes, we believe a more forward-looking assessment will become increasingly important alongside the argument that adverse effects from previous rate hikes have yet to materialize. In particular, the question will be to what extent households, businesses, and financial institutions can absorb further increases in interest rates. Occupation-Level Evidence For our third approach, we consider labor market outcomes for 25 occupations that were exposed to significant technological disruption (e.g., photo processing, proofreaders, file clerks), which we identify (both in terms of occupations and timing) based on historical anecdotes and our internal large language models. Given that these occupations were selected as cases where technology had the largest impact on labor demand, the observed headcount reductions are likely upper bounds for technology-driven labor displacement from AI. That said, the observed dynamics may be informative for how AI will impact labor market dynamics for workers in the most exposed occupations. Exhibit 7 shows headcount reductions in these occupations in the five years after employment started to decline in response to a technological innovation. We find that among these occupations, employment fell by around 25% on average, suggesting that very large job losses are possible when technology makes labor redundant. More importantly, we again find that the gross hiring rates declined and gross job separations increased following technological disruptions, but that the labor adjustment was again more skewed toward an increase in separations. The bigger decision is the guidance The more consequential question is what Treasury says about the path beyond November. Repeating the current language would provide predictability but risks tying Treasury's hands as the next increase in aggregate coupon issuance approaches. We would favor replacing "at least the next several quarters" with "the coming quarters" and referring to "overall" nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes. These seemingly modest changes would materially increase Treasury's flexibility. "Coming quarters" preserves near-term predictability without unnecessarily extending the no-change commitment, while "overall" distinguishes aggregate coupon issuance from individual-tenor auction sizes. That flexibility matters because the next increase in coupon issuance is getting closer. If sizes remain unchanged through 2027, estimates imply roughly $975bn of net bill issuance to private investors in CY27, around $430bn more than in 2026. The bill share of debt would rise from 23.1% in 2026 to 25.4% in 2027 and 28.4% in 2028. This does not require higher coupon sizes today, but suggests aggregate nominal coupon sizes may need to begin rising around the middle of next year. Source: Citi Research Source: Citi Research, OilX The effective tanker fleet is considerably smaller than headline capacity suggests, with sanctions, idling and war-related damage compounding logistical bottlenecks. Sanctioned vessels now represent over 20% of the approximately 2,400 crude oil tanker fleet and nearly 5% of the more than 10,700 product tanker fleet. Moreover, crude oil tanker idling increased from just over 5% in 1H’26 to 8% in 3Q’26 and almost 9% QTD. Tanker incidents have exceeded 250 YTD, versus 170 in 2025 and a five-year average slightly above 200, with war damage accounting for approximately 40%. In particular, of the global VLCC fleet of over 930 vessels, only 784 are currently in service, with more than 100 idled and the remainder employed in storage, detained or damaged. Some 170 VLCCs are sanctioned, of which only slightly more than 80 regularly operate. NIOC controls nearly 40 VLCCs, but only around half are currently active. These constraints highlight the gap between nominal tanker availability and effective carrying capacity; see Fig. 6 for a detailed split of the effectively available VLCC fleet. records.text: nsibilities: The House is largely responsible for originating tax and spending bills, conducting oversight of agency programs, and initiating investigations and impeachment hearings. The Senate has similar legislative and oversight responsibilities, but is specifically tasked with confirming executive branch appointments including the Supreme Court and the Federal Reserve Board and conducting impeachment trials. It is viewed as more deliberative and stable than the House, and regularly tempers more extreme legislative efforts. ‘I’m just a bill’: Once written and cleared through committee, most legislation must first clear a simple majority in the House. In practice, legislation typically needs to meet a 60-vote threshold in the Senate in order to avoid the filibuster. The major exception is the “reconciliation” process which can be used to pass tax, spending, or a debt-limit bill via a simple majority vote; this process can be used only once a fiscal year for each of those priorities. Republicans used that process to pass the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (2017) and the OBBBA (2025); Democrats used it to pass the American Rescue Plan Act (2021) and Inflation Reduction Act (2022). From there, the President can sign the bill into law or can veto it, sending it back to Congress. To override a veto, the bill must pass both chambers by a two-thirds majority. While a simple majority (51) is required to pass a bill, the effective threshold is 60 to end debate and avoid the filibuster. Centrists in both parties have mattered more in recent years. Centrist Democratic senators in swing states (PA, AZ, and MI) could play the same moderating role as other centrists. A Senate flip would increase the chances that vacancies on the Federal Reserve or Supreme Court go unfilled in 2027-28. Former Fed Chair Powell’s term will end in January 2028, though he could stay on indefinitely until a successor is confirmed. There is already bipartisan support for the Fed’s independence, which we see as limiting the pool to conventional picks. Asset purchases | Further down the road: At some point, the ECB would need to introduce asset purchases to inject more excess liquidity. They will be introduced to limit the upward pressure on ESTR from refinancing operations growing too large, and to ensure alignment with DFR. We think that a trigger point could come around 4Q28, when the combined take-up in refinancing operations (standard and structural) reaches around €600 billion. Therefore, the ECB could still decide to keep the characteristics of the structural asset portfolio vague given its implementation is, at the earliest, in our view, in two years. And that timeline could be pushed back further if the ECB decides to adjust the QT pace. We have noted previously that any new portfolio would likely take the form of a fully risk- shared, capital key-guided portfolio, similar to the APP (except for the risk sharing) and likely tilted to shorter maturities (see here). The speeches from Schnabel and Välimäki confirm our thinking around the maturity composition being on the shorter side (due, for instance, to interest rate risk and stance neutrality). We note that the size of the outstanding universe will put a limit on how short the maturity composition can be. The ECB will have to respect an issue share limit of 33% for public-sector bonds and 50% for supranational bonds (see here).

records.text: The rise in the unemployment rate due to a technology shock understates the total amount of labor displacement, however. Some workers that are displaced may find jobs relatively quickly (thereby limiting the increase in the stock of unemployed workers), while others may decide to exit the labor force (thereby limiting the rise in the unemployment rate via a reduction in the denominator). A better measure of technology-related labor displacement is therefore the impact on gross job losses (and gains). In Exhibit 4, we therefore extend our analysis to examine how a 1pp increase in productivity due to a positive technology shock (identified the same way as above) impacts gross job losses and gross job gains. We again estimate that each 1pp increase in productivity raises the unemployment rate by 0.3-0.4pp, with the increase driven by a 0.5-0.6pp cumulative increase in the gross job loss rate and a smaller 0.2pp drag on gross hiring. The sum of these cumulative flow estimates are higher than the peak increase in the unemployment rate, which confirms that labor force exits or quick rehiring limits the rise in unemployment, even when automation is occurring. Under our baseline forecasts that AI-related efficiency gains will ultimately deliver a 15% gross boost to economy-wide productivity, these estimates imply that up to 9% of workers could be displaced during the AI transition, with an additional headwind from slower hiring weighing on overall employment by 3%. Third-quarter results across major US and European banks pointed to solid top-line performance, led by outsized strength in equities trading. Our review of earnings call commentary illustrates that AI remains both a financing tailwind and a growing risk-management focus for banks. The scale of hyperscaler capex, data center investment, and related power infrastructure needs continues to support healthy pipelines across IG corporate bond underwriting, structured project finance, and private credit syndication. This heightened focus on risk management supports our view around the durable premium embedded in AI-related CDS, as it remains the primary hedging tool for market participants. records.text: Oil Monitor 22 October 2026 Citi Research 2 The normalization of Arab Gulf oil exports has been volumetric rather than logistical, with unprecedented shipping inefficiencies keeping delivered crude costs elevated despite recovering flows. AG-China VLCC freight rates recently approached $250/t, equivalent to roughly $35/bbl and more than 20x the average level seen over the previous decade. According to one shipping client, extended waiting times for STS transfers in the Arab Gulf, together with vessel repositioning, are effectively removing around 5% of global VLCC capacity from the market. Meanwhile, rising Arab Gulf exports have contributed to push on-water crude oil levels to 1,350-m bbl, which combined with longer haul voyages, have driven a sharp increase in ton-mile demand. As a result, the recovery in physical oil flows has not translated into a comparable normalization of delivered supply costs. Figure 1. But recent labor market n data show some signs of AI-related hiring headwinds, and market participants are increasingly focused on whether AI labor cost savings will be sufficient to justify investment. In this Global Economics Analyst, we consider three empirical approaches to quantify how technology has historically displaced labor and the implications for AI labor disruption. First, aggregate shocks imply that each 1% increase in labor productivity due to n technological innovation leads to a temporary 0.3-0.4pp peak boost to the unemployment rate that fades after two years. This rise is driven by a 0.5-0.6% cumulative increase in gross job losses and a smaller 0.2% drag on gross hiring. Second, industry-level productivity shocks imply very similar effects on n unemployment and gross job gains and losses, but larger impacts on job losses in the late 1990s and following larger productivity shocks. Third, examining 25 occupations that were exposed to significant technological n disruption (e.g., photo processors, proofreaders, file clerks) implies larger job losses (25% on average after five years) when technology makes labor redundant. AI under different scenarios Divided Congress: Democratic control of the House alone could increase AI oversight via investigations into prominent AI firms, knock-on effects on utility costs, and an increased focus on the data-center buildout. Democratic sweep: This scenario would put AI safety, testing, and transparency standards firmly on the agenda. Labor-market concerns and protections would also likely move to the forefront. Over the medium term, perhaps the most important issue at the press conference will be how Governor Ueda distinguishes between signaling a faster pace of rate hikes and raising the terminal rate itself. Interest among some market participants in a neutral interest rate above 2% has been increasing. However,“shortening the time to the next move” and “raising the ultimate destination of the rate-hiking cycle” are not necessarily the same issue. " As in July, some Governing Council members may well ask whether a hike should be discussed at the October meeting. Our base case, however, is that a majority will prefer to be patient and wait until December to take a better-informed decision. This is especially likely given that back-to- back hikes could be read by markets as a sign that the ECB believes it is falling behind the curve and is stepping up the pace of tightening. Several factors underpin this reasoning. First, as highlighted above, the recent tightening in financing conditions driven by higher long-term rates will help dampen inflation, giving the ECB room to be patient. Second, the December projections will allow the ECB to refine its assessment of the 2027 growth and inflation outlook by incorporating member states' fiscal plans. Finally, they will also extend the forecast horizon to 2029, shifting the medium-term focus to 2028-2029, when the volatility induced by the energy component should fade. 22 October 2026 8 Barclays | ECB preview

While a simple majority is required in the House, 60 votes are needed in the Senate to avoid the filibuster on funding bills. It isn’t clear that 7 Democrats will join Republicans in order to do that, particularly if control of Congress was set to flip in a few weeks. In 2018, Democrats gained control of the House during Trump’s first midterms, but a border-wall funding dispute meant that the House did not approve a bipartisan spending package that had passed the Senate. The government closed for a 35- day shutdown, the longest until the record 43-day shutdown in Oct-Nov 2025. Debt limit and defense supplemental budget: If control of the House and/or Senate are set to flip to Democrats in 2027, Republicans are likely to attempt to use the remaining time to (1) act on supplemental defense spending worth roughly USD60billion, which is less than the USD350 billion sought by the President for defense priorities, and (2) lift the debt limit into 2029, past the 2028 election. The debt limit can be raised via reconciliation. If successful – which isn’t guaranteed given the tight margin in the House – Republicans would remove it as a potential point of leverage for Democrats in budget negotiations over the next two years. Survey data for the third quarter suggest that this resilience extended into the summer. In 2022 NW Europe had limited LNG import capacity2, as the region had historically relied on pipeline gas imports as its primary source of gas supply. As a result, when NW Europe tried to replace curtailed Russian pipeline gas with incremental LNG imports in 2022, it quickly ran into bottlenecks, driving TTF higher, at times more than 60 EUR/MWh above Asia LNG prices — in sharp contrast with its typical modest regional discount — to trigger domestic gas demand destruction to help balance the market (Exhibit 2). Since the September meeting, there has been little economic data that would compel the BoJ to deliver a consecutive rate hike, while the exchange rate has remained stable thus far. Against this backdrop, in this Global Economics Analyst, we use three different empirical approaches to revisit how technology has historically displaced labor. Our results continue to suggest that AI automation will deliver significant time and labor cost savings, but that the timing and extent of automation and labor disruption will likely track the overall economic cycle. Historical Data Still Suggests Meaningful Headwinds to Job Growth Aggregate Evidence Our first approach builds upon our work from last year which considered how the impact of a technology-driven increase in productivity impacts the unemployment rate. After spending much of the 1980s and 1990s grappling with debt crises and policy mistakes, many emerging economies spent the early 2000s implementing structural reforms, consolidating pu blic finances, and generating primary fiscal surpluses. As a result, gross government debt averaged just 35% of GDP in 2007. Today, that figure has climbed to around 75%. One might argue that emerging-market debt still looks attractive relative to the much heavier debt burdens found across the developed world. However, these economies are classified as emerging markets for a reason. Emerging markets typically operate with weaker institutions, lower tax capacity, and less policy credibility than advanced eco nomies. Consequently, the level at which debt becomes a market concern is often considerably lower than in developed countries. Among the investable EMs, the BRICS economies, excluding Russia, are among the most indebted. China tops the list, with gross government debt approaching 90% of GDP. Yet China is in a cycle of its own, as policymakers try to offset private-sector deleverag ing with fiscal stimulus, much as Japan did during its long post -bubble adjustment. We also revisit ownership statistics for French debt. Spooky vibes. As Halloween rolls around, the fear factor across the market spectrum is tangible with AI-related jitters, credit market concerns and the OAT-Bund widening train dragging other EGB spreads along with it. The flight-to-quality in Bunds and DSLs has returned with ASW spreads widening again. Furthermore, the return of Bunds' safe-haven status has seen its relationship with the synthetic energy price index completely break down in recent days ( Figure 1). The energy complex is soaring higher but the market is shrinking the rate hike premium on the sharp widening in EGB spreads and the overall tightening in financing conditions, thus benefiting Bunds. For the ECB Governing Council, which meets next week, this is an uncomfortable position. On the one hand, the escalating conflict and the surge in energy prices into the winter have pushed the latter's levels above the adverse scenario modeled at the ECB's September forecast round. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures History shows that divided governments under Democratic presidents are often defined by fiscal restraint, such as in the 1990s under Clinton and the 2010s under Obama. However, the same is not true under Republican presidents – for example, in 2019 under Trump and during the 2000s under Bush. While our base case is for the fiscal deficit to average about 6.3% of GDP in 2027–28, remaining relatively stable from 2026, it would not take much to widen it into the 7–8% range (see lower chart). Our base case already embeds a modest increase in defense spending, higher interest costs, and recent developments on the tariff front. We anticipate must- pass legislation will largely extend status-quo funding levels but see paths to more generous defense spending priorities paired with additions on the non-defense side, namely the reversal of some social and healthcare spending cuts contained within 2025’s OBBBA. Fiscal consolidation – such as tax hikes or spending cuts – is unlikely, in our view. Discretionary spending is already at the low end of historical ranges, while cuts to mandatory social safety net, healthcare and defense priorities are unpopular. Due to doubts over the AI trade and renewed concerns about Chinese competition, foreign investors continued to withdraw from both the Korea and Taiwan stock market (Figure 2). We believe key driver s behind this divergence are (1) the difference in exporters’ USD selling pressure and (2) differences in central bank rhetoric. According to the CBC’s data, the share of Taiwan’s export proceeds immediately converted into TWD fell to a year-to-date low of 1.71% in September, pointing to weaker exporter conversion demand (Figure 3) . In particular, the central bank highlighted that w hile exports increased 69.7% year -on-year, immediate conversion into TWD rose by only 7%. Macro/CTA funds are less short duration Source: Bloomberg, Barclays Research As we look ahead, attention next week will turn to the October FOMC meeting, when the Fed is widely expected to remain on hold (only a 2bp hike is priced in). For markets, the key question is how recent developments have shaped the policy outlook. Inflation has been firmer than expected; our economists estimate core PCE rose 0.35% m/m in September and now expect the Fed to hike twice, in December and January. Against that, financial conditions have tightened somewhat. Figure 6 shows that, since the September meeting, credit spreads have widened and the USD has strengthened, even as energy prices have fallen and the expected policy-rate path is little changed. How Chairman Warsh explains the decision to stay on hold will therefore be key. If he emphasizes the noise in monthly inflation readings and the improvement in the breadth of inflation, markets are likely to interpret the message as dovish. In contrast, if he stresses that the Fed simply needs more data before judging whether the recent inflation strength is persistent, the message would be more neutral and leave the door open to the hikes our economists expect in December and January. records.text: ering dollar amount, but the rise in government indebtedness has been a global phenomenon since the Global Financial Crisis (GFC). Across advanced economies, gross government debt climbed from a little over 60% of GDP before the crisis to about 110% today. Japan remains the world's most indebted major economy by a wide margin. For years, that burden attracted surprisingly little scr utiny because the Bank of Japan absorbed a large share of government bond issuance. Once inflation returned, however, investors began paying closer attention to the sustainability of Japan's fiscal position. Figure 1: The Global Rise of Sovereign Debt Source: State Street Markets, IMF In the United States, the debt measure most commonly cited by the Treasury, federal debt held by the public, stands at roughly 100% of GDP. The IMF's broader gross debt measure, however, already exceeds 120% of GDP. The difference largely reflects Treasury securities held by government trust funds, most notably t he Social Security Trust Fund. Those trust funds have historically been steady buyers of Treasuries, providing a captive source of demand. Over the coming years, however, as Social Security's cash balances are drawn down, that support is expected to diminish, gradually turning the trust fund from a net buyer into a net redeemer of Treasury securities. This adjustment alone contributes an estimated 35bp to 10y yields. As do long-term rate expectations: Next, we model the Fed response to additional fiscal stimulus next year. As increased fiscal spending carries the risk of adding further cyclical upside to the economy, it suggests up to two more rate hikes from the Fed next year (to five hikes total, from our current baseline of three). Taking the 60% beta that 10y rate expectations have had with fed funds since 2000, additional Fed tightening could contribute a further 30bp to 10y yields, bringing the total impact to roughly 65bp. Rate hikes increase the Treasury’s interest expense: But this may still underestimate the market impact from more spending. This is because current issuance is heavily overweight the front-end. This makes it such that additional Fed rate hikes would transmit to budget deficits more rapidly and persistently than in a counterfactual scenario featuring a more balanced issuance profile. On the equity channel, the outperformance of US equity markets over the rest of the world YTD is largely driven by tech outperformance. Such an outcome we think would be USD negative, despite the historical pattern of the USD typically outperforming in risk-off environments. This is due to two reasons. Second, foreign investors have demonstrated a more active approach to their FX hedging of US equities. As US stock-FX correlations rise, which we anticipate will occur in an AI-related drawdown, foreign investors are likely to increasingly hedge their USD exposure. It is generally viewed as more deliberative and stable than the House, and regularly tempers more extreme legislative efforts. Legislation: Once written and cleared through committee, most legislation must first clear a simple majority in the House. In practice, legislation typically needs to meet a 60-vote threshold in the Senate in order to avoid the filibuster. The major exception is the reconciliation process, which can be used to pass a tax, spending, or a debt-limit bill via a simple majority vote; this process can be used only once a fiscal year for each of those priorities. Republicans used that process to pass the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (2017) and the OBBBA (2025); Democrats used it to pass the American Rescue Plan Act (2021) and Inflation Reduction Act (2022). From there, the president can sign the bill into law or veto it and send it back to Congress. To override a veto, the bill must pass both chambers by a two-thirds majority. In practice, that significantly constrains what a Democratic Congress could pass after the midterms. History suggests Republicans start at disadvantage: The incumbent president’s party typically loses seats in Congress. records.text: European Rates Weekly 22 October 2026 Citi Research 3 Unanchored OAT-Bunds can move on little, with contagion becoming meaningful. The challenge for the ECB is that OAT-Bunds are already in uncharted territory when it comes to idiosyncratic risk premium with growing signs of contagion, especially to Belgium – Figure 3 and Figure 4. With the OAT-Bund spread adrift from typical fundamental drivers, there is no anchor level in the near- term. It’s become a confidence game. The growing sensitivity greatly increases the risks around ECB wording. President Lagarde – who may be leaving her position early - has experience when it comes to talking about spreads in a fragile market from the early days of her leadership in 2020 (and the infamous “not here to close spreads” line). The legacy to avoid is bookending the presidency with elevated levels of spread volatility. That means the words will need to be chosen extremely carefully, likely spoken from script. The ECB may not be able to bring near-term relief to OATs, but the challenge is to not make the situation any worse. Figure 3. Page 2 Press conference Assuming the Fed does not raise rates, the key focus of the press conference will likely be on why they chose to hold. In our view, the September FOMC meeting set up a strong baseline for skipping October and raising rates again in December. The dot plot showed 16 out of 18 officials expecting at least one more hike this year, but only four anticipating 50bps more in 2026. Communications from several key officials, including Vice Chairs Williams and Jefferson, indicated that there was limited urgency in tightening further, even if more hikes were likely. At his recent IMF appearance, which occurred after the CPI report, Warsh indicated that the economy has evolved broadly in line with their expectations from September, even though the latest inflation data was described by several officials as disappointin g. Consistent with this, Warsh could indicate that they received limited new data since the last meeting and believed they could benefit with a little more time to assess underlying trends. There are other factors that could support hold ing rates steady at this meeting. Financial conditions have started to tighten, though they remain accommodative on many metrics. Officials might want to see how much FCI tightening occurs for reasons outside of monetary policy before taking further action. Alternatively, as in April, she could say that she has a broad sense of the direction of travel but that incoming information will continue to guide decisions within the ECB's established monetary policy framework. A high bar to amend the ECB's balance sheet policies At the press conference, President Lagarde will inevitably be asked whether the ECB could intervene to help ease governments' borrowing costs, particularly in France. We expect her to say that the rise in long-term rates, not only in France but globally, will be factored into the ECB's updated assessment in December through its impact on growth and inflation. We also expect her to reiterate that the ECB remains attentive to the broader range of financial stability risks. The “New Deal” programs of the 1930s and the “Great Society” initiatives of the Johnson administration in the 1960s stand out as notable and expansive programs passed by unified governments. More recently, key stimulus programs and tax legislation have also passed during unified governments, including the 2025 OBBBA. The American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 passed via the slimmest of Democratic majorities in the House and Senate. Narrow majorities after the 2016 election facilitated the passage of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA). records.text: Revisiting the Extent and Timing of AI Labor Displacement Concerns of imminent AI-related labor displacement have cooled in recent months after hitting a fever pitch this spring. As shown in Exhibit 1, the number of layoffs attributed to AI has pulled back sharply from its peak this spring. On a similar note, the number of news reports on AI-related job losses surged through May but has since fallen back to levels seen at the start of 2026. As we noted in our most recent AI adoption tracker, the labor market impacts from AI remain visible but narrow. Job growth in the most AI-exposed industries continues to underperform by around 10k relative to its long-run trend over the last 3 months (consistent with the underperformance over the last several years), although this has been roughly offset by increased hiring in AI-related construction jobs. Cross-sectional industry-level patterns are starting to show some signs of AI-related hiring headwinds from AI adoption, however. As shown in Exhibit 2, the correlation between adoption and unemployment has turned positive (and statistically significant) in the service sector, while the correlation between AI adoption and job growth has turned slightly negative (albeit not statistically significant). While these patterns suggest that a modest labor market headwind is emerging, the near-term headwinds remain smaller than feared earlier this year. Looking ahead, the midterm elections may fundamentally alter the fiscal landscape through two primary channels: 1) the potential for a reconciliation bill during the lame-duck session, and 2) in the event of a blue sweep, additional non-defense and defense spending negotiated to keep the government open in 2027. In our upside fiscal risk scenario for next year, our modeling suggests that 10y yields could rise by a further ~65bp. FX: The major risks around the midterms - a downward correction in AI sentiment and a worsening fiscal position – would both put downward pressure on the USD, in our view. Should markets reassess the outlook of the AI buildout, we think it would be USD negative, despite the historical pattern of the USD typically outperforming in periods of risk-off. This is for two reasons. For one, foreign investors have become more active in their allocations to US equities in recent years, implying scope for active selling if US equities were to underperform. Second, foreign investors have demonstrated a more active approach in their FX hedging of US equities as well. As US stock-FX correlations rise, which we think they would in an AI-related drawdown, foreign investors are likely to increasingly hedge their USD exposure. Given the US’s large need for foreign funding, a US-centric ‘fiscal-risk shock’ is another unwelcome headwind, suggesting risks to the USD are asymmetrically skewed lower into year-end. records.text: ns than a decrease in hiring for these occupations. We draw three conclusions from our results. First, under our forecast for a 15% n productivity increase from AI, around 9% of workers could be temporarily displaced during the AI transition. Second, employment reductions are on average more driven by job losses than slower hiring, suggesting that AI-related layoffs should provide a good real-time guide. Third, our industry-level and occupation-level analyses suggest upside risks to labor disruption. Narrow labor impacts so far reflect the fact that the AI transition is still in early n stages, but also that the overall economy has remained resilient. All three of our empirical approaches imply that automation-related labor disruption is limited when the overall economy is healthy but accelerates during cyclical slowdowns. We therefore expect that the AI labor market transition will be manageable under our baseline forecast where activity remains healthy, but that AI-related labor disruptions could well amplify the broader business cycle. The session includes a key deadline on 11 December, when government funding expires and a shutdown would start if no new funding authority is in place. Shutdown possible in echo of 2018: Republicans will still control Congress though 3 January, but they will need Democrats’ help to prevent a shutdown after 11 December. While a simple majority is required in the House, 60 votes are needed in the Senate to avoid the filibuster on funding bills. records.text: Cash and equity account for a larger share of deal consideration Across both markets, the share of cash-only consideration has declined in 2026, while mixed cash-and-equity structures have increased slightly (Exhibit 5). Cash consideration does not translate mechanically into bond issuance, as it can be funded through balance-sheet liquidity, bank debt, or bonds. But the shift toward more mixed consideration is modestly more credit-friendly, as it reduces the extent to which acquirers need to fund transactions entirely with cash. That said, M&A debt supply has still been elevated, especially in the USD market. Year to date, M&A-related supply has reached $177 billion in USD IG and $55 billion in USD HY, equivalent to 10% and 20% of total gross issuance, respectively (Exhibit 6, top panel). This is toward the higher end of the recent historical range and partly reflects the lagged financing of transactions announced last year. By contrast, in the EUR market, M&A supply totals €11 billion in IG and €10 billion in HY, equivalent to 2% and 12% of gross supply, respectively (Exhibit 6, bottom panels). While this is an increase from the very low levels of recent years, it remains modest, particularly given the strength of European M&A activity. Maintaining current sizes while increasing issuance elsewhere would gradually reduce the long end's share of total issuance without requiring abrupt changes to benchmark auctions. Buybacks should remain flexible We expect Treasury to continue signaling maximum long-end buyback sizes of at least $4bn, with $6bn announced ahead of individual operations, while retaining flexibility to increase sizes where liquidity conditions warrant. The evidence currently points to greater need in the 10-20y sector than the 20-30y sector. Offers in each of the last two 10-20y operations rose above $40bn, while recent 20-30y offers have been around $10-15bn. This argues for targeted flexibility rather than uniformly larger buybacks across the long end. Market implications For markets, the critical distinction is between auction sizes and guidance. Unchanged November auction sizes could disappoint investors expecting long-end cuts. But less restrictive guidance should partially offset that disappointment by keeping future changes to both aggregate issuance and maturity composition in play. The more bearish outcome would be for Treasury to keep auction sizes unchanged while simply reiterating the existing "at least the next several quarters" language.
